# AeroGlobe {.page-title}

[In active development · data pipeline & 3D visualization]{.kicker}

A browser-based 3D globe for flight tracking. It is a work in progress, and an early version is live. The pieces described here exist today, and the parts marked as planned do not.

::: {.actions}
[Open the live site](https://exios66.github.io/aeroglobe/){.btn .primary} [View the code](https://github.com/Exios66/aeroglobe){.btn}
:::

::: {.caveat}
**Work in progress.** The repository is being built right now, so this page will change. It describes the state of the code on 23 October 2026. The [live site](https://exios66.github.io/aeroglobe/) shows a short sample of real traffic, three OpenSky observations recorded when the site was built, and a labeled sample day of generated flights. It does not poll live data, and no real historical day is published yet.
:::

## The problem

Most flight trackers show what is in the air now. I wanted to look at flights that have already happened: where an aircraft went, how a route looked over a day, and what a busy hour of global traffic looks like on a globe. That is a data problem before it is a graphics problem. Bulk historical flight logs are large, free and awkward, and a live API gives you only a short window.

My first version was live-first, polling an API every 15 seconds. Auditing it showed that a historical view needs a different shape: process the data ahead of time, publish it as static files, and let the browser do the rest.

## Approach

{{< include ../partials/diagrams/_aeroglobe.qmd >}}

The client is React and TypeScript with CesiumJS for the globe. State lives in Zustand stores, and search and filtering work on a set derived from the flight store. A small Express server proxies the live feed for local development.

The data side is a Node and TypeScript pipeline. It takes state vectors, turns them into per-aircraft tracks, splits each track into flights, slices the tracks into hourly chunks and writes a catalog. The output is plain JSON that a static host can serve, so there is no database and no always-on API. The pipeline puts a size limit on each hourly chunk and throws an error when a chunk goes over it.

## What I built

- **The globe client.** A Cesium viewer with aircraft markers, search, filters for region, altitude, status and airline, a flight detail card, a flight list and a dark and light skin.
- **A static data pipeline.** Normalization, flight segmentation, hourly chunking and a catalog, with a snapshot command that records a few OpenSky observations and a fixture command that writes a deterministic set of generated traces for offline work.
- **A historical source.** An adapter for full days of adsb.lol flight data, which runs through the same pipeline and can publish to a separate data branch from my own machine. A global day needs about 10 GB of disk.
- **Playback and track replay.** A day picker and a time slider with play and pause, driven by the globe's clock, that moves every aircraft along its recorded positions. A **Replay track** control follows one selected aircraft, with an option to keep the camera on it. Up to 2,000 aircraft nearest the camera draw a short trail from their consecutive observations.
- **Reference data.** Airport and airline tables built from public sources, with the source and licence of each recorded next to the file, and time-zone polygons for the planned overlay.
- **Tests and checks.** The repository's continuous integration runs lint, the type-checker, the tests and the build on pushes and pull requests to the main branch.

## What is planned

The design spec for the next stage is a draft. In outline:

- a published historical day on the live site;
- a faster playback engine that decodes data off the main thread and draws aircraft as one layer, with a transport bar that sets the speed and shows traffic over the day;
- inferred routes between airports and a time-zone overlay;
- a per-aircraft history panel;
- a personal flight logbook kept in the browser.

None of these is built yet beyond the basic playback above, and the spec may change as I build.

## What I'm learning

- Choose where the work happens before choosing the framework. Moving the heavy work into a build step is what makes a historical view possible without running a server.
- Fixtures are worth building early. Because the pipeline can run on generated traces, every stage has a test that needs no network.
- An audit of my own first version was more useful than adding features to it.
